[38;5;246m❯ [38;5;231mWrite a 350-word story about a fox, no tools, plain text.[39m                                                                        
[49m                                                                                                                               
[38;5;231m⏺[39m Mara and the Firefly                                                                                                     

  Mara was the smallest fox in the Hollow Wood, and the only one who was afraid of the dark. The others hunted at midnight with
  bright, unblinking eyes. Mara lingered at the mouth of her den, ears flat, watching the shadows pool between the birches.
                                                                                                                    
  "You'll starve," her brother said, trotting off. "Night is when the mice come out."
                                                                                                                             
  So Mara went hungry for three nights. On the fourth, her stomach overruled her fear, and she crept into the woods.
                      
  Every sound was a threat. A snapped twig became a wolf. A hanging vine became a snake. She froze beside a fallen log, heart
  hammering, certain she would never move again.
                                                                                                                              
  Then she saw it: a faint green glow, drifting low between the ferns. A firefly, lost and blinking, no bigger than a seed.

  Mara watched it wobble through the air. It was not afraid. It simply lit the few inches around itself, and then a few inches 
  more, and kept going.                                                   

  She followed. The firefly's light showed her a root to step over, then a patch of moss, then a mouse-trail worn smooth in the 
  leaf litter. Each glow was small, but each was enough for the next step.

  By the time the moon cleared the treetops, Mara had caught two mice and a fat beetle. The firefly rested on her nose, blinking   
  proudly.  
                                                                                                                         
  "I thought the dark was one big thing," she whispered.
                                                                                                                                
  The firefly flickered, which she took to mean: It's only a lot of little things, and you only have to see the next one.    
                                    
  After that, Mara still felt her heart quicken when the sun went down. But she no longer waited at the den's mouth. She stepped   
  out, found the nearest patch of glow (a firefly, a puddle of starlight, the pale underside of a leaf) and walked toward it.
                                                                                                                           
  Her brother never understood how the smallest fox in the Hollow Wood came to know the night better than anyone, himself included.

  She just smiled, a small green light still blinking on her shoulder. "I only ever look at the next step, little brother."
